lead: A blockchain can be public, private or consortium. The label comes from three permissions: who may read the ledger, who may write a transaction, and who may validate a block. This matters because a chain for Bitcoin payments and a chain for three banks share data differently. Public chains let anyone join; private chains are open only to one organisation; consortium chains share control among a known group. Banks, land registries, supply chains and enterprise pilots use these labels to state trust and access rules before choosing a platform.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 on features and Chapter 1.3 on decentralization.

blocks.text: A blockchain type is mainly a permission rule, not a product name. Three questions decide it. Read permission: who may see the ledger and its history? Write permission: who may submit a transaction? Validate permission: who may check transactions and append a block? The set of nodes allowed to append is the validator set.

A public blockchain is open on all three. Anyone may read, submit a transaction and join the validator set. It is permissionless because no gatekeeper approves entry. Bitcoin is the standard example: anyone can run a node, and miners compete to append blocks.

A private blockchain is controlled by one organisation. Read access may be open or limited. Write and validate access are given only to approved nodes. It is permissioned: membership is by invitation or approval. A company with 12 offices may let all 12 validate, but the company still sets the rule.

A consortium blockchain, also called a federated blockchain, is shared by several organisations. No single member owns the rule alone. A known group, such as 3 banks, approves members and validates blocks. It is permissioned. Some systems mix public read with private write; treat that as a hybrid mix, not a fourth basic permission rule.

Trust differs. A public chain trusts open rules and costly consensus. A private chain trusts the owning organisation. A consortium trusts shared membership rules. Speed and cost differ too: public proof-of-work chains are slow and energy-heavy; permissioned chains with known validators can confirm faster and cheaper, but only inside that group.

Privacy follows read permission. A public ledger exposes transactions to all readers. Permissioned chains may restrict readers to approved members, but a private chain can also allow public read while keeping write and validation closed; the type label alone does not fix read access. Governance also changes: public changes need broad node or miner agreement; private changes follow one organisation; consortium changes need the group's rule. Hyperledger Fabric is a permissioned platform used for private or consortium networks; its details belong to Unit 6.

sections.h3: Choosing a type without mistaking private for closed

blocks.text: Permissioned does not mean centralized by default. A private or consortium chain can run many nodes, copy the ledger and validate by rule. What is controlled is membership: an administrator or a group approves who joins. Centralisation would mean one node can rewrite history alone. A well-built permissioned chain still checks blocks against shared rules and signatures.

items: List who must read the ledger. If unknown outsiders must read, check whether public read is acceptable.
List who may write. Separate customers who only view records from staff who submit updates.
List who validates. One organisation points to private; several organisations point to consortium; an open set points to public.
Check governance: who adds or removes validators, and whose signature changes the rule?
Check legal privacy needs. Personal records may need restricted read even if validation is shared.

blocks.text: Some syllabi use public, private and consortium as the three types. In practice, the deciding question is who validates. A chain with 13 validating offices under one registrar is private. A chain with 3 validating banks under a shared rule is consortium.

figure.caption: A decision tree sorts a chain by who validates. The private branch carries the land-registry example with 13 validating offices, and the consortium branch carries the trade-finance example with 3 validating banks.

spec.aria: A decision tree asks who validates: anyone means public with Bitcoin, one organisation means private with 13 validating offices, several organisations means consortium with 3 validating banks.

examples.question: A land registry has 1 registrar and 12 sub-registrar offices. Citizens may read records but not write them. The registrar and all 12 offices can validate updates. A trade-finance chain is run equally by 3 banks; each bank validates. Choose the blockchain type for each case. Give one reason from the validator set.
steps: Count the land-registry validators: 1 registrar + 12 sub-registrar offices = 13 validating offices.

All 13 offices belong to one government department, and one administrator sets membership. Citizens may read, but write and validate are closed. The deciding rule is write and validate, so this is a private permissioned chain.
The 3 banks are separate organisations. No single bank owns the rule; they share governance. This is a consortium permissioned chain.
Public is not chosen: citizens do not validate land updates, and the banks are a known closed set.
examples.answer: Land registry: private permissioned chain with 13 validating offices. Trade finance: consortium chain with 3 validating banks.

traps: Calling a private chain 'not blockchain' because it is permissioned. It still uses blocks, hash links and shared validation.
Assuming public is always better. Public gives open access but often costs more and runs slower; private gives control but trusts the admin more.
Saying permissioned means centralized. Many nodes can validate; only membership is controlled.
Confusing a consortium with a public chain that has many users. A consortium is a closed set of organisations with shared governance.
Treating read and write permission as one. Citizens may read a land ledger but not write to it.

quiz.a: A public blockchain allows anyone to read, submit transactions and join validation without approval. It is permissionless.

quiz.q: Why can a permissioned chain still be called a blockchain?
quiz.a: It stores transactions in linked blocks, copies the ledger across nodes and validates blocks by shared rules. Permission controls membership; it does not remove blocks or validation.

quiz.q: Four hospitals share a chain. Each hospital validates; patients may read their own records. Which type fits?
quiz.a: Consortium permissioned chain. The validator set has 4 separate organisations, so control is shared, not owned by one hospital.

quiz.q: Compare trust in a public chain and a consortium chain.
quiz.a: A public chain trusts open rules and costly consensus; anyone may join, so it resists gatekeeper control. A consortium trusts shared membership rules among known organisations; it is faster and more private but depends on the group's governance.
The set of nodes allowed to check transactions and append blocks to the chain.

quiz.q: A company has 12 offices, but only the head office validates. Which type?
quiz.a: Private permissioned chain. One organisation controls membership and validation, even though 12 offices exist.

quiz.q: Why does a public proof-of-work chain often cost more per transaction than a permissioned chain?
quiz.a: Public mining spends energy and hardware on open competition. A permissioned chain validates among known nodes with lighter consensus, so it usually needs less energy and confirms faster.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, these labels appear in platform selection, legal contracts and audit rules. Newer systems mix public settlement with private execution, so search for 'hybrid blockchain', 'permissioned ledger governance' and 'consortium governance' next. Enterprise courses often focus on consortium chains because several firms must share one ledger without one owner.
